newsitem.title: REPUBLIC OF IRELAND: Irish bonds fall back after five-year auction.
newsitem.headline: Irish bonds fall back after five-year auction.

text.p: Irish government bonds weakened in afternoon trade on Tuesday, underperforming gilts and bunds after a 150 million punt auction of the 6.5 percent bond due 2001, dealers said.
The auction was covered 2.16 times and had a tail of one basis point but dealers said there was little follow-through interest.
"The market weakened dramatically after the auction. There was no interest whatsoever in the shorts in particular and the market just went offered," one dealer said.

Traders said that short-dated paper had rallied early in the day and short yields had fallen by 12-13 basis points, helped by a strong performance from the UK gilt market after Eddie George's comment on Monday that the need for a UK rate hike was less urgent than thought in December.
But the strong early performance by Irish bonds proved short-lived as the market fell back after the auction.

"This morning's auction was the victim of a squeeze. The short-end of the curve was up almost 40 pence going into it and that seemed to take the edge off. A few would-be participants perhaps shied away from it all," one dealer said.
Underperformance by other European peripheral bond markets may also have contributed to weakness in Dublin, traders said.
"I think that's another factor explaining why the Irish market is doing less well this afternoon. There's a bit of divergence out there as regards peripherals," a trader said.
By 1630 GMT, the six percent bond due 2001, the auction stock, was at 103.15 to yield 5.70 percent, down 40 pence on the day and well off the average auction price of 103.82.
Further out the curve, 10-year paper was also weaker with the eight percent bond due 2006 quoted at 111.30 to yield 6.37 percent, down 30 pence from Monday's close.
Attention tomorrow will focus on U.S. January consumer price data, due at 1330 GMT and expected to show a rise of 0.3 percent on December and 3.2 percent on January last year.
Dealers said they will also be keeping an eye on UK January retail sales data and its impact on sterling.

The British currency fell by five pfennigs on Tuesday, relieving some of the upward pressure on the Irish pound in the ERM grid. Traders said it should dissipate recent market talk of a revaluation of the Irish pound.
"Revaluation is a possibility if sterling goes to 2.95 or 3.00 to the mark but it's not going to happen at current levels," said Padhraic Garvey, economist at Riada Stockbrokers.

"If the central bank had aggressively sold punts, driven up the foreign exchange reserves and we were at 14.99 percent above the weakest currency in the ERM grid, then a revaluation is the option to take but in the current circumstances it's not," he said.
